name: Fremantle
title: Ship Thickness Measurement Fremantle | Kwinana & Henderson UTM
description: Thickness gauging at Fremantle and Kwinana for bulk carriers, container ships, livestock carriers and offshore vessels: hull, tanks, holds and piping.
h1: Hull and Tank Gauging for Ships at Fremantle, Kwinana and Henderson
intro: Fremantle is Western Australia's main general-cargo port: container ships, car carriers and livestock carriers work the Inner Harbour at the mouth of the Swan River, while bulk carriers and tankers use the Kwinana jetties in Cockburn Sound. Many deep-sea ships trading here will dock next in an Asian yard, so a Fremantle call is a practical moment for a pre-docking steel estimate or an owner's condition check. For every job, our technicians fly from India to Perth and join the vessel; nobody is stationed at the port.

highlights.h: Grain and bulk at the Kwinana jetties
highlights.p: Bulk carriers loading grain or discharging fertiliser at Kwinana often lie alongside for several days. Ballast tanks, deck plating, hatch coamings and holds not yet in use can be gauged around cargo work, giving the owner condition data before the ship sails for Asia.

highlights.h: Henderson floating dock for smaller vessels
highlights.p: The floating dock and vessel transfer system at the Australian Marine Complex in Henderson serve naval and commercial work. Smaller vessels docked there, such as offshore support ships, tugs and workboats, can have bottom plating, sea chests and tank structure gauged while dry.

Live sheep exports by sea are legislated to end on 1 May 2028, so owners of the livestock carriers loading at Fremantle face redeployment, sale or conversion decisions. Condition gauging of livestock decks, their supporting structure and the ballast tanks gives a factual basis for that choice.

port.h: Fremantle and Kwinana: two harbours on the Indian Ocean coast
p: Fremantle Ports operates two harbours. The Inner Harbour lies in the mouth of the Swan River beside the old port town, with container terminals on North Quay and car-carrier, passenger and livestock ships at the other Inner Harbour berths. The Outer Harbour lies to the south in Cockburn Sound, where the Kwinana jetties serve the grain terminal, fuel imports and a range of bulk cargoes for the industrial strip ashore. Ships approach from the Indian Ocean inside Rottnest Island and wait at Gage Roads or at the anchorages in Cockburn Sound. Tides on this coast are small, so they rarely decide a berthing; wind does. A strong sea breeze builds on summer afternoons and winter cold fronts push swell into Gage Roads, and either can delay pilot boardings, the berthing of high-sided ships and launch transfers to the anchorage.

Traffic follows Western Australia's economy. Container ships bring consumer goods and equipment into the state, car carriers discharge vehicles, and livestock carriers load sheep and cattle for the Middle East and Asia. At Kwinana, bulk carriers lift wheat, barley and canola through the grain terminal, with the busiest loading months following the harvest that begins late in the year, while product tankers discharge fuel and other bulk ships handle fertilisers and industrial cargoes. Cruise ships use the passenger terminal through the southern summer. Two changes are coming: the sea trade in live sheep is legislated to stop on 1 May 2028, and the state's Westport programme plans to move container handling from the Inner Harbour to a new terminal at Kwinana over the longer term. Both will reshape which ships call, but neither changes the case for knowing the condition of the ones that do.

For ship inspection, the key fact is that Western Australia has no commercial dry dock that deep-sea bulk carriers and container ships normally use. Ships trading here dock in Singapore, China or elsewhere in Asia, so a Fremantle or Kwinana call is often the last chance to collect readings before a docking is planned and a steel figure goes into the specification. Smaller vessels are a different story. The Australian Marine Complex at Henderson, on the eastern shore of Cockburn Sound, gathers shipbuilders and repairers such as Austal, BAE Systems and Civmec around a common-user facility with wharves, a floating dock and a vessel transfer system, used for naval sustainment and commercial work. Offshore support vessels, tugs and workboats from the North West Shelf and the metropolitan coast can be maintained there, and their dockings are a natural time for gauging.

facilities.h: Kwinana jetties, Inner Harbour berths and the Henderson complex
p: Most Fremantle gauging is done alongside during cargo work. At the Kwinana jetties a bulk carrier loading grain or discharging fertiliser can often give access to ballast tanks, deck plating, hatch coamings and any hold not yet in use; the job is planned with the master around the loading sequence and the terminal's rules on who may be on deck. Inner Harbour calls by container ships and car carriers are shorter, so the scope narrows to deck structure, coamings, lashing bridges, ramps and accessible tanks. Livestock carriers are best gauged between voyages, when the pens are empty and washed out. At Gage Roads and in Cockburn Sound a waiting ship can be boarded by launch, provided the sea state allows a safe transfer.

Docking-period work happens at Henderson. The common-user facility at the Australian Marine Complex is owned by the state and run under contract by Ventia, and each company in the precinct applies its own site rules, so names, qualifications and equipment lists go to the yard well ahead of the team. A smaller vessel lifted on the floating dock or moved ashore by the transfer system can have its bottom and side shell, sea chests, tanks and piping gauged with full access. For deep-sea ships heading to an Asian yard, the useful Fremantle product is a pre-docking estimate: readings on the spaces most likely to need renewal, so the owner can negotiate the steel quantity before the ship arrives.

context.h: AMSA inspections, biosecurity and the livestock trade
p: Port state control in Australia is carried out by the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), which belongs to both the Tokyo MoU and the Indian Ocean MoU. A large share of AMSA's boardings are on bulk carriers, reflecting the country's export trades, and structural defects feature often: wasted hatch coamings and cover panels, holed air pipes and ventilators, corroded hold ladders and rails, and fractured frames. AMSA has also refused port access for a period to ships with repeated serious failings. A thickness record that shows where a ship stands against its allowable diminution helps a master and superintendent answer an inspector's questions about suspect plating, and it gives the owner warning before a deficiency turns into a detention.

Biosecurity rules sit alongside the safety rules. Since 15 June 2022 international vessels arriving in Australia have had to report how they manage biofouling through the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry's Maritime Arrivals Reporting System, with a management plan, recent cleaning or an approved alternative as the accepted routes, and the same department enforces Australia's ballast water management requirements. Sea chests and other niche areas are where biofouling collects and where corrosion often runs fastest, so they deserve readings at every docking. Livestock carriers face their own regime: AMSA certifies ships for the carriage of livestock under Marine Order 43, and the condition of decks, ventilation trunks and drainage is part of that picture. With the sheep trade ending in 2028, owners of these ships are already weighing their options.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs we see at Fremantle and Kwinana
jobs.p: Fremantle jobs fall into three groups. The largest is pre-docking and condition gauging on bulk carriers and container ships that will dock in Asia, planned for the days a ship spends alongside at Kwinana or in the Inner Harbour. The second is livestock carrier work, where owners want hard numbers on decks and tanks before deciding how a ship will trade after 2028. The third is docking-period gauging at Henderson on offshore support vessels and harbour craft, where access is good and the scope can be complete. We agree the scope with the superintendent, book access through the agent or the yard, and travel from India once the berth or dock date is firm. Reports follow the class TM formats.
list: Pre-docking steel estimate on a Supramax bulk carrier loading barley at Kwinana before a Chinese yard docking, covering topside and hopper tanks and the hold frames most exposed to grab damage
Condition gauging of livestock decks, deck girders and double-bottom tanks on a converted livestock carrier between voyages, to inform a sale or redeployment decision
Docking survey readings on an offshore support vessel on the Henderson floating dock: bottom plating, sea chests, tank tops and seawater piping
Pre-purchase gauging of a car carrier during an Inner Harbour call, concentrating on the weather deck, internal ramps and ballast tanks
Scrubber wash-water and overboard pipe gauging on a container ship alongside at North Quay, with crack detection at the shell penetration

logistics: The team flies into Perth Airport, with connections from India, and reaches Fremantle, Kwinana or Henderson by road. Indian technicians need an Australian visa suitable for short-term specialist work, applied for before travel, so its lead time is planned in from the first enquiry. Terminal and berth access goes through the ship's agent; because visiting technicians do not hold a Maritime Security Identification Card, they work under the escort or visitor arrangements each terminal sets. Henderson yards run their own inductions, and launches to Gage Roads are booked by the agent.
vessels: Bulk carriers loading grain or discharging fertiliser

faqs.q: Can a bulk carrier be gauged while it loads grain at Kwinana?
faqs.a: Usually, if the scope is matched to the loading plan. Ballast tanks that have been emptied, ventilated and tested can be entered, deck plating and hatch coamings can be read between loader moves, and holds can be gauged before they receive cargo. We work through the master's loading sequence so the team is never in a space that is about to be filled, and the most important readings are taken first.

faqs.q: Is there a dry dock in the Fremantle area for a large merchant ship?
faqs.a: Not for deep-sea bulk carriers or container ships, which normally dock in Southeast Asia or China. The floating dock at the Australian Marine Complex in Henderson suits smaller vessels such as offshore support ships, tugs and workboats. For a large ship, the practical approach is to gauge the likely problem areas during a Fremantle call and send the figures to the Asian yard before the docking.

faqs.q: Can thickness gauging be done at the Gage Roads anchorage?
faqs.a: Yes, when the weather allows. A ship waiting at Gage Roads or in Cockburn Sound is boarded by a launch booked through the agent, and in ballast it can open tanks and holds for gauging. Winter fronts and swell can stop transfers, so anchorage work is planned with a fallback: if the launch cannot run, the scope moves to the berth once the ship comes alongside.

faqs.q: What should be gauged on a livestock carrier before its future is decided?
faqs.a: Start with the structure that livestock trading wears hardest: the livestock decks and their supporting girders, drainage and effluent tanks, the plating around fodder and water systems, and the ballast tanks below. Add the weather deck, hatch coamings and any spaces that would matter for a conversion to another trade. The result is a factual condition record the owner can put in front of a buyer, a charterer or a yard.

faqs.q: Does Australia's biofouling regime change when gauging should be done?
faqs.a: Not directly, because biofouling reporting concerns hull cleanliness rather than steel thickness. It does make sea chests and other niche areas more visible to owners, and those spaces are among the worst for corrosion. When a ship is docked, whether at Henderson or in an Asian yard, we recommend adding sea chest plating, grating supports and the adjoining shell to the gauging scope.
